Zainab, you asked why I turned down that scholarship from the trader. Sit, I'll tell you. I'm Gurpreet. In my second year, Ramlal-ji, a cloth trader from our town, paid my hostel fees. He said it was nothing. But every Sunday afterwards he rang: "Who are your friends? Why was your mark low in physics?" Once he said, "After all I've spent, you should be in the library, not at that match." I began to hide my phone. I felt watched, and I felt I owed him my whole life.
Around then, my old teacher, Mrs Iyer, quietly paid my exam form fee, handed me the receipt and said, "Don't mention it, it's done." I remember standing straighter.
I repaid Ramlal-ji in small parts over three years, and thanked him each time. It was the first time in my life I felt free of him.

qa.q: Who paid Gurpreet's hostel fees in the second year?
qa.a: Ramlal-ji, a cloth trader from Gurpreet's town, paid the hostel fees.

qa.q: What was Gurpreet feeling after the Sunday phone calls began?
qa.a: Gurpreet felt watched and obliged, hiding the phone and feeling as though a whole life was owed. The questions about friends and marks felt like ownership, not help.

qa.q: What choice did Gurpreet make that eventually gave a sense of freedom?
qa.a: Gurpreet repaid Ramlal-ji in small parts over three years and thanked him each time. That let the help become something finished, not a hold on Gurpreet's life.

qa.q: How might Ramlal-ji have seen his Sunday calls?
qa.a: Probably as caring interest, and perhaps as his right after paying the fees. For Gurpreet they felt like being watched, which shows how help can mean different things to giver and receiver.

grounding: A student receives help that comes with watching and expectation, and contrasts it with a clean gift that lets the receiver keep dignity.

Two nights before the project deadline, Keerthana's laptop stopped turning on. She had no money for a repair and the college lab closed at six. Neelam, a senior from the hostel, handed over her own. "Take it. Just return it Sunday."
Keerthana finished the report at 3 am, weak with relief. But on Saturday Neelam texted, "Remember I helped you. Come to my society event tomorrow. Bring your friends." On Sunday, "Why are you always with those girls? I lent you my laptop, you know." Keerthana's stomach tightened each time her phone buzzed.
She returned the laptop that afternoon with a small card: "Thank you. It saved my project. I'll come to the event if I can, but I can't promise more." Neelam stared at the card, then said, "I only wanted to help." Keerthana nodded. "I know. I'd still like to say no when I need to."

"Need a lift?" Kashish called from a grey hatchback.

I'm Simran, and I used to answer every kindness with an apology. When I moved into my first flat, Zubin from next door came over to see if I needed a drill. "Sorry, I'm such a bother," I said. "I should have bought my own. I'm useless at this." His face did a small flinch, and he mumbled that it was no trouble and left quickly.
A month later, I needed help hanging the shelves. This time I knocked on his door and said, "Zubin, I could really use your hands for twenty minutes. Thank you for offering before."
He grinned and came over with the spirit level. We finished before the tea cooled. I asked nothing more of myself than to say a plain thank you, and I noticed how much easier it felt for both of us.

qa.q: What did Zubin first offer Simran when she moved in?
qa.a: He came over to see if Simran needed a drill.

qa.q: What was Simran feeling when apologising the first time?
qa.a: Simran felt anxious about being a bother, with a habit of putting herself down. By the second time, a plain thank you felt easier.

qa.q: What did Simran do differently the second time she needed help?
qa.a: Simran knocked, asked directly for Zubin's help and said thank you, without belittling. That made it easy for Zubin to say yes.

qa.q: How does Zubin probably see Simran's second request compared with the first reaction?
qa.a: He probably feels valued and useful, as his grin and quick arrival suggest. His flinch the first time suggests the apologies left him awkward and unwelcome. 😊

grounding: A person who thanks a neighbour simply instead of apologising lets the giver feel useful.

Bidisha's first pay had gone straight to her parents. Every month since, she sent part of her salary to Kolkata, and lent to friends who asked. By the fourth month she was checking her bank app before buying lunch, and she had started to dread Shalini's calls.
On Sunday, Shalini rang again. "Just until the month end, Bidi."
Bidisha looked at her notebook, where she had finally listed what she needed for rent, food, and one small saving. She breathed. "Shalini, I can lend you a little this once. After that I can't keep lending. I have to keep some for myself."
There was silence. "I didn't realise it was hard for you," Shalini said, quieter. "Okay. I'll ask my cousin for the rest."
Bidisha put the phone down. She felt lighter, and a little sad.

Manoj, your mother says you've tried the band, the yoga club and the debate society in one year. Sit. I'll tell you about my sixteenth year. I'm Ujjwal, and I tried it all. I joined a rock band and quit after two months, spent a season in student politics, learned chess, and once stopped speaking to my friends for a week because I'd decided they were shallow.
My father said I was wasting my life. But my aunt said, "Let him look." I went from one thing to the next, and in the middle of all that mess, I began helping the small children at the mohalla library learn to read. I stayed. That one stuck, and I taught for forty years.
Nobody could see the search from outside. Inside, it was the hardest work I'd done.
